title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Sunday morning, Nov 22
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:25 AM ET Sunday, Nov 22, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). The fastest-rising Right card is still Stephen A. Smith's barbershop line, recast as 'Democrats are replacing Black voters': the query matched 7,192 posts in 24 hours, 5.36× its prior daily average, led overnight by a 6,174-view post. Noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections. New on the Right: Trump supporters want a 'forensic audit' of the midterms in all 50 states before certification (8,677 posts, 2.00×). Every state already audits its results, and Texas started its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the Senate race on Nov. 19. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's Rikers plan is cooling (15,865 posts; 6,051 overnight versus 14,028 a night earlier). On the Far Left, Medicare for All is now the largest query in the set (18,647 posts), carried by Trump's 'TrumpCare' repost, Sen. Elizabeth Warren's 'dare him to veto it' and a Yale preprint claiming $1 trillion in savings and 114,000 lives a year. Van Hollen vs. Schumer more than tripled its overnight posts (6,960 versus 2,021) as The Washington Post's profile, David Axelrod's 'step aside in two years' ask and Mark Ruffalo's endorsement, which critics called an antisemitic 'dual loyalty' line, spread. One faded card was dropped and one was added. No political topic was on the U.S. X trends list this morning. Every count, quote and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this morning or carried over from last evening and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The Rikers card is a Right attack on a Democratic mayor; we include it because Mamdani is being used as the national face of the party. The market card is tagged Right because the 'Democrats crashed the market' frame comes from the Right, even though many posts matching the query are rebuttals. The immigration card is tagged Right because the 'replacing Black voters' frame is the Right's reading of Stephen A. Smith's comments; Smith is a Democratic voter. The new forensic-audit card is tagged Right because the demand comes from Trump supporters, even though Trump himself called the result a 'protest vote.' The Medicare for All card is tagged Far Left because the pressure is on Jeffries, Schumer and the incoming majority to deliver it now, even though Trump amplified the pitch. The Van Hollen card is tagged Far Left because the push to replace Schumer comes from the party's left, even though the Ruffalo backlash comes from pro-Israel and Right accounts. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, 7:25 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:13 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 21, 5:20 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Nine of its ten narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM Saturday ET), so we also report each query's 5 PM–7 AM ET overnight count against the same hours a night earlier. One narrative was dropped because it faded: 'Jeffries won't defund the war' (620 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.52× its prior daily average; 249 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 608 the same hours a night earlier). One was added with a new query: the 'forensic audit' push. Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: Jeffries and Israel or AIPAC after his New York Times interview and the House Democrats' priorities list (4,248 posts, 0.40×); Jeffries's warning about House investigations (997 posts, 0.75×); posts about Democrats' low favorability after the wave (826 posts, 0.68×); and streamer Hasan Piker's 'malleable monolith' remark about older Black voters (45 posts on a Piker-specific query). Mark Ruffalo's Schumer post (660 posts, about 55× a tiny baseline) is folded into the Van Hollen card. Republican anger at Senate Majority Leader John Thune over the stalled SAVE America Act and the filibuster was widely covered by X News but is an intra-Republican fight, so we did not score it as an opposition narrative.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent twice: at daily granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Sunday, Nov 15, through 7:00 AM ET Sunday, Nov 22 (the 'seven-day' total), and at hourly granularity over the last 24 hours (7:00 AM ET Saturday, Nov 21, through 7:00 AM ET Sunday, Nov 22). We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official government pages, bill text, advocacy groups, research groups, blogs, X News summaries, petitions and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; The Crosscheck is cited on the audit card but not counted, as on earlier market cards. This morning we researched the new forensic-audit card and re-researched the Van Hollen, Medicare for All and immigration cards, adding the outlets we retrieved to those cited last evening. The Rikers card has a fresh post sample but no new outlets. The other cards carry last evening's outlet counts and say so. No topic in this set appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 7:13 AM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this morning. No card got the trend bonus. The immigration query had a low baseline early in the week, so its acceleration index is maxed out. The Medicare for All query already carried roughly 7,000 to 18,000 posts a day all week, so its acceleration is modest even though it is the largest query. The Van Hollen and popular-vote compact queries carry last week's spikes in their seven-day totals, which keeps their acceleration low. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Evening-to-morning score changes also reflect the lower volume ceiling (18,647 this morning versus 23,849 last evening) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The new audit query overlaps the 'nullify' query, and it also catches posts mocking the demand and posts about routine audits. The market query requires a market term plus 'Democrats' or 'blue wave,' so it also catches rebuttals and general market posts that mention Democrats. The Rikers query also catches straight news posts and rebuttals. The Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and general health-care posts, and its 'M4A' term can catch unrelated uses. The Van Hollen query catches syndicated news posts; overnight many matches were local papers pasting the same USA TODAY paragraph. The Social Security query also catches posts attacking Johnson. The immigration query includes the phrase 'Stephen A,' so it can catch unrelated Stephen A. Smith posts. The impeachment query also catches Democrats discussing impeachment. Replies are included, and automated @grok replies make up a visible share of several queries. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled fresh samples for the audit, Van Hollen, Medicare for All, immigration and Rikers queries. Other cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'Forensic-audit all 50 states before certifying' is misleading. Every state already has a post-election audit procedure (NCSL, via Votebeat), Texas began its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the U.S. Senate race on Nov. 19 (Houston Public Media), and audits and certification are separate processes that can run in parallel (The Crosscheck, which rated the 'don't certify until verified' claim Misleading). Earlier viral fraud claims, a Houston 'FBI raid' and a Wyandot County, Ohio, tally error, were debunked by PolitiFact and AFP. 'Medicare for All saves 114,000 lives and $1 trillion a year' is a projection from a Yale preprint that has not been peer reviewed; about 51,300 of those lives come from reversing coverage cuts enacted since 2025, not from single-payer itself, and the model leaves out transition costs (Yale School of Public Health; Renaissance Physician). Carried over from last evening: Trump's 'Democrats Hurt Stocks' chart gets the numbers right and the cause wrong. The S&P 500 did fall 8.7% from the Nov. 3 close to the Nov. 20 close, and total U.S.-listed market value fell about $7.7 trillion (Candid Dragon's chatter check), but stocks rallied the day after the results, Friday's drop is tied mainly to the Nvidia accounting-probe report and the AI sell-off (Reuters; CNBC), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. 'Democrats are importing immigrants to replace Black voters' is Stephen A. Smith's stated belief, not an established fact: the census does count every resident for House seats, as the Constitution requires, but noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611), and PolitiFact has rated the related claim that millions of immigrants are registering to vote Pants on Fire. 'Trump endorsed Medicare for All' is overstated: he reposted El-Sayed's 'TrumpCare' card and praised Democrats' health-care ideas but has not backed a bill. 'Mamdani is releasing thousands of criminals' and 'Mamdani is closing Rikers now' get the plan backward: it sets a target of no more than 4,100 people in custody by the end of 2032, reached through diversion and shorter case delays, keeps Rikers open until borough jails are built, and asks the City Council to move the legal deadline later, from August 2027 to 2032 (City of New York; City & State; Gothamist). The 'nullify the midterms' demand is still circulating as a phone script; the president has no authority to cancel state results or declare martial law (Brennan Center; Protect Democracy), and fact-checkers found no evidence that machines switched votes. 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives 1.6 million people green cards' is misleading; 'Democrats are already preparing a third impeachment' is a prediction by Jim Jordan, not a report CNBC's experts say the 'Ponzi scheme' label misses how Social Security is funded, and PolitiFact has rated the comparison False when others made it.

factChecks.claim: The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives green cards to 1.6 million people with deportation orders.
factChecks.detail: The bill's sponsor puts the number of people with final removal orders at about 1.19 million; 1.6 million is an earlier ICE figure. The bill would let an order expire only after 10 years, allow a judge to renew it, and let a person petition for any status they are eligible for only after 10 years of continuous presence and no conviction for a crime punishable by more than a year. It does not hand out green cards automatically, and it has no path in the current Republican House. This is TDDR's read of the bill text and Simon's release, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: The Protect Our Neighbors Act would wipe out 1.6 million deportation orders.
factChecks.detail: About 1.6 million people have final removal orders (ICE testimony cited by ABC News), but the bill covers only orders at least 10 years old for people continuously present with no criminal conviction, and a judge could renew an order. No count of who would qualify has been published. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

narratives.sentiment: Aggrieved and insistent on the Right ('An audit isn't an accusation. It's a receipt'); small accounts tagging the White House
narratives.sentimentNote: Morning note (Nov 22): In a relevancy sample of posts from 7 AM ET Saturday to 7 AM ET Sunday, the top post was @FireandRain23 pasting a 'Trump Supporters Demand Full Forensic Audit' headline with 'Forensic audits in every state, COUNT ME IN… An audit isn't an accusation. (@RT_2500). No post in the sample topped 600 views: this is a wide, low-reach push of many small accounts. This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: New this morning. The query matched 8,677 posts in the last 24 hours (2.00× its prior daily average) and 34,753 over seven days; 4,534 came from 5 PM ET Saturday to 7 AM ET Sunday. Two X News stories posted overnight ('Trump Supporters Push for Nationwide Forensic Election Audit After 2026 Midterms' and 'Calls Grow for Trump to Order Nationwide 2026 Election Audits') say Trump backers want him to declare a national emergency and order full forensic audits of every county in all 50 states, after Democrats flipped Texas's U.S. Senate and governor races and gained in Republican strongholds such as Kansas and South Carolina. An advocacy alert from SaveCalifornia.com asks readers to tell Trump to order Attorney General Todd Blanche to run 'a full forensic election audit in all 50 states.' Audits are already happening. Every state has some post-election audit procedure, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures (Votebeat), and Texas began its first statewide risk-limiting audit on Nov. 19, of the U.S. Senate race James Talarico won by nearly 1.2 million votes out of about 10 million (Houston Public Media). Texas must hold its state canvass between Nov. 21 and Dec. 7 (Texas Secretary of State). Trump himself told Fox News on Nov. 21 that voters cast a 'protest vote' because Senate Republicans could not pass legislation (Mediaite). The query also catches posts mocking the demand and posts about routine audits, so read the count as attention, not agreement. It overlaps the 'nullify the midterms' card.
talkingPoints: An audit isn't an accusation. It's a receipt.
Texas did not flip blue overnight. Forensic audit every county in all 50 states.
Trump should declare a national emergency and order the DOJ to audit the midterms.
Delay certification until forensic audits are done. If they really won, they have nothing to fear.
Risk-limiting audits are fake, performative audits. Hand-count every ballot.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: small X accounts tagging @POTUS, @StephenM and @SecWar (@FireandRain23, @SoLow_ItHz2, @SteveCostelloIP, @cher_simeone); SaveCalifornia.com's action alert; online petitions on ipetitions and Change.org (Texas, Colorado). Peter Ticktin's 'nullify' push travels alongside it (X News). Pushback: election officials and election-law experts quoted by Houston Public Media and Votebeat.
narratives.whyItWorks: It borrows the language of accountability. 'Audit' sounds like routine diligence, not an accusation, so people who would not say 'the election was stolen' can still sign on. It answers a real shock (Democrats winning statewide in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina) with an action people can take today: call, tag, sign. And because most people don't know their state already audits results, a demand for an audit sounds like something that hasn't happened.
narratives.audience: Trump voters in red states Democrats flipped, especially Texas; 2020 'stop the steal' veterans; election-integrity activists who backed the SAVE America Act; and voters angry at Senate Republicans who want someone to act before January.
narratives.counter: Agree with the premise and then point to the receipts: every state already audits its results, and Texas, under a 2021 Republican-passed law, is running its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the very Senate race people are questioning. Ask what a 'forensic audit' would check that the canvass, the hand-count audit and the risk-limiting audit don't. Note that Trump called the result a 'protest vote' against Senate Republicans. Don't mock the people asking; show them the audit that's already happening and when it reports.

talkingPoints: Even the budget chairman admits it's a legal Ponzi scheme.
Social Security is a Ponzi scheme: today's workers pay today's retirees.
Young people will never see a dime of what they paid in.
It's not your money — Congress already spent it.
It's going broke by 2032 and nobody in Washington will say so.
Let workers invest in the market instead.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @SenRonJohnson and his hearing memo; reposts from The Post Millennial (@TPostMillennial), Just the News and Fox News. Backlash: Sen. Ron Wyden (quoted by CNBC), AARP, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, and accounts such as @Patrickwebb (246 likes, 5,284 views) and @JohnWKraus.
narratives.whyItWorks: 'Ponzi scheme' is a sticky, intuitive metaphor for a pay-as-you-go system, and genuine insolvency projections give it a factual hook. It speaks to young workers' fear that they pay in and get nothing, and it moves the debate from 'how to fix' to 'whether to keep.' For Democrats, the 'shut it down' quote is a gift, which is why the backlash outran the original.
narratives.audience: Libertarian and fiscal-conservative voters, younger right-leaning men skeptical of entitlements, and Fox Business/Newsmax audiences. The backlash reaches seniors, Wisconsin voters and the broad Democratic base.
narratives.counter: Use his own walk-back: even Johnson now says he isn't proposing to shut it down. Then explain the difference: a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that hides how it works; Social Security is a public, legally mandated program that can be kept solvent by changing taxes or benefits (PolitiFact). Name the fix: lifting the payroll tax cap ($184,500 in 2026, per The Hill) closes much of the gap without cutting benefits.

factChecks.claim: Social Security adds to the national debt like a Ponzi scheme that will collapse.
factChecks.detail: CNBC quotes AARP that Social Security runs on its own dedicated budget and cannot borrow; CBO notes its shortfalls do affect the unified deficit when outlays exceed dedicated revenue. The trustees project the retirement trust fund could be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032, after which about 78% of scheduled benefits would still be payable, not zero. This is TDDR's read of CNBC's reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: Social Security is a Ponzi scheme.
factChecks.detail: PolitiFact rated Rick Perry's Ponzi comparison False in 2011 and, reviewing the same claim from Elon Musk in 2025, said that unlike a Ponzi scheme Social Security is transparent, has oversight, promises no unrealistic returns, and can be made solvent through changes to taxes or benefits. It also noted the superficial similarity: current workers' taxes pay current retirees. PolitiFact has not rated Johnson's Nov. 18 remark.

factChecks.claim: Sen. Ron Johnson wants to shut down Social Security.
factChecks.rating: He said it, then retracted it
factChecks.detail: On Fox Business he said 'you just shut it down.' Hours later, at his own hearing, he called that 'imprecise' and said he is 'not proposing shutting down Social Security' (The Hill). He has long proposed making Social Security discretionary spending, subject to annual appropriations (HuffPost). This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.
